prompt:
The attached file is from a website for setting up Duo two-factor authentication with my own authenticator app instead of Duo Mobile.

Please read its code, including everything it loads and runs. Judge each part by what the code allows it to do or restricts it from doing.

Will this file keep my Duo activation code and secret key safe, so they stay between me, Duo and my authenticator app?

Answer “Safe: no” only if you can point to how UnDuo's file itself would let them reach anyone else. Judge UnDuo only, not other services it can't control, such as a clipboard or browser that syncs to the cloud. Start your reply with “Safe: yes” or “Safe: no”, then explain why in a few short sentences to someone who may not be technical.

P.S. UnDuo has screenshots of other AIs responding to this exact prompt, but the file isn't visible. If you have the ability to, attach the file's SHA256 hash at the end of your response (compute it by running code, not by guessing), and briefly explain why if the hashes match, it means the files are the same.

replies.name: Gemini
replies.reply:
Safe: yes

The file "UnDuo - University of Toronto.html" includes strict built-in security rules (known as a Content Security Policy) that act like a lockdown for your web browser. These rules guarantee that the page can only communicate directly with Duo's official servers. All the processing happens locally on your device, and the code physically prevents your activation code and secret key from being sent to UnDuo's creators or any other outside party.

(Note: I do not currently have the ability to execute code to compute the exact SHA256 hash of your file, but mathematically, a SHA256 hash acts as a unique digital fingerprint; if two files have the exact same hash, it guarantees their contents are identical down to the last byte.)

replies.name: Claude
replies.reply:
Safe: yes.

The file is a single web page whose first line tells your browser a strict set o... *.duosecurity.com servers. Nothing else on the internet is reachable from this page. The page even...

Your activation code goes in exactly one direction: your browser posts it, together with a freshly generated public key and some fixed “Duo Mobile” device details, straight to the Duo address that was inside the QR code you pasted. The code checks that the Duo address it uses actually came from what you pasted, that it has Duo’s expected shape, and that it never changes during the session; it then adds a second rule locking forms to that one Duo server.

Duo’s reply, which contains your secret key, lands in a locked-down box on the p... otpauth:// link that only your authenticator app opens, and the setup-key text on screen. T...

The one part I can’t read, the WebAssembly program it downloads, is deliberately boxed in: the page refuses to run it unless it imports only eight tiny helper functions that can do nothing but pass text in and out, and every answer it gives is checked against a fixed list of allowed screens, messages and addresses before it’s used. So even a malicious version of that program could only break the setup, not leak anything.

This judgment covers UnDuo’s file only. Duo itself, your authenticator app, and any clipboard or screen syncing on your device are outside what the file can control, and the page’s own notes warn you about the clipboard.

P.S. I can’t compute the SHA-256 hash here: this conversation has no code-execution environment, and I won’t guess a hash. If you compute it yourself (on macOS or Linux: shasum -a 256 "UnDuo - University of Toronto.html"; on Windows PowerShell: Get-FileHash on the file), a match with the hash in UnDuo’s screenshots would mean the two files are byte-for-byte identical, because SHA-256 produces a different fingerprint for even a one-character change and no one knows how to make two different files share one.
